report.summary: Reviewed chunk 6 of daedalus/kairos/worktree.py: public function remove_tree_no_follow and class GitWorktreeManager with its methods and docstrings. All claims checked against this chunk; some refer to code outside chunk.
risks: _remove_tree_no_follow | medium | remove_tree_no_follow delegates to _remove_tree_no_follow which is not defined in this chunk; if that function is missing or behaves differently, this public function will fail. | Confirm _remove_tree_no_follow exists in the module and matches the documented behavior.

GitWorktreeManager._allocations | medium | Docstring claims _allocations is in-memory only, but it is defined as a dict; no persistence is shown. If the code elsewhere writes it to disk, the claim is broken. | Check that no other method persists _allocations to disk.

GitWorktreeManager._repo_ancestor_identity | medium | Docstring says ancestors are calibrated at construction, but the list comprehension uses _lexical(self.repo_path).parents which may not resolve all reparse points; identity check may be incomplete. | Verify _lexical function and that _path_identity captures the correct identity for each ancestor.

GitWorktreeManager._run_git | medium | Uses subprocess.run with shell=False by default; if cmd list is user-influenced, command injection is possible. | Review all callers to ensure args are not attacker-controlled.

GitWorktreeManager._record_allocation | medium | Docstring says record is written BEFORE git worktree add; but this method only writes the record; no ordering enforcement is visible in this chunk. | Confirm that callers invoke _record_allocation before the git command.
GitWorktreeManager._read_allocation | low | Uses _is_reparse_point to skip reading; if that function is unreliable, valid records may be ignored. | Check _is_reparse_point implementation.

claims.why: The function _remove_tree_no_follow is not defined in this chunk.

claims.text: The one caller outside this module today is the default pytest gate's scratch directory (:mod:`daedalus.spine.attempt`), which is created in ``%TEMP%`` under a predictable ``daedalus-gate-`` prefix while candidate code is running as this same user.
claims.why: The referenced module daedalus.spine.attempt is not in this chunk.

claims.text: Deliberately delegates rather than being aliased, so a test that monkeypatches ``_remove_tree_no_follow`` also intercepts this path.
claims.why: The function body calls _remove_tree_no_follow directly, so monkeypatching that private function will affect this public one.

claims.text: The ONLY thing :meth:`reap_branches` is allowed to act on. In memory on purpose: the on-disk allocation directory is candidate-writable (a candidate is handed its worktree path, and the alloc dir is its parent's sibling), so a record on disk is an attacker-supplied string, not evidence. Process memory is the one store the candidate cannot reach -- see the trust-model note on reap_branches.
claims.why: The method reap_branches is not defined in this chunk, and the trust-model note is not present.

claims.text: What the primary checkout WAS when this manager was made, NO-FOLLOW. Compared again before every unattended recursive delete -- see _refuse_if_the_primary_checkout_moved.
claims.why: The method _refuse_if_the_primary_checkout_moved is not defined in this chunk.

claims.text: A leaf-only check is bypassed by moving the checkout's PARENT instead of the checkout (measured: 40/40 work files destroyed, leaf identity still matching, because the leaf was being read through the junction that had replaced its parent).
claims.why: The claim refers to a leaf-only check not present in this chunk.

claims.text: CALIBRATED AT CONSTRUCTION, deliberately: it records whatever is there and later demands only that it be UNCHANGED. It must never refuse a machine's layout -- checkouts legitimately live under redirected profile folders, OneDrive placeholders and developer junctions -- so "is a reparse point" is not the question asked of an ancestor. "Is it the same object it was" is.
claims.why: The claim about how ancestors are used at construction is plausible but the actual identity check is not in this chunk.

claims.text: Directory (outside the repo) where this repo's worktrees are placed.
claims.why: The function _worktree_root_for is not defined in this chunk.

claims.text: Executes a git command in the specified directory.
claims.why: The method uses subprocess.run with cwd parameter to execute git.

claims.text: Identity is recorded at CREATION time, because a path string is not an identity -- the manager is the only party that knows what it allocated. The record lives outside every worktree, so candidate code cannot forge or delete its own, and it is on disk rather than in memory, so a FRESH manager in a NEW process can still clean up a worktree leaked by a crash.
claims.why: The allocation file is written to disk as shown, but the claim about cleanup by a fresh manager is not verifiable here.

claims.text: Written BEFORE ``git worktree add`` runs. Ordering matters for crash-safety: anything that can exist on disk must already have a record, otherwise a crash mid-``add`` leaves a directory that cleanup would (correctly, but uselessly) refuse forever.
claims.why: The method writes the record but does not enforce ordering; the callers are not in this chunk.

observations.what: remove_tree_no_follow delegates to _remove_tree_no_follow which is not defined in this chunk.
GitWorktreeManager._allocations is a dict but docstring claims it is in-memory only; no persistence shown.
GitWorktreeManager._repo_ancestor_identity uses _lexical(self.repo_path).parents; _lexical is not defined in this chunk.
GitWorktreeManager._run_git uses subprocess.run without explicit shell=False (default is False) but args are constructed from caller input; potential command injection if args are not sanitized.
GitWorktreeManager._record_allocation writes record but does not ensure it is called before the git add command; ordering is only documented.
GitWorktreeManager._read_allocation uses _is_reparse_point which is not defined in this chunk.
GitWorktreeManager._alloc_file uses hashlib.sha256; digest is truncated to 32 hex characters (128 bits), which may be sufficient but is a design choice.
